what_its_for: Ramucirumab is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of cancer, including stomach cancer, a type of lung cancer called non-small cell lung cancer, colorectal cancer (cancer of the colon or rectum), and liver cancer. It works by blocking a protein that helps tumors grow new blood vessels, which cuts off the blood supply the cancer needs to grow and spread.
how_to_take: Ramucirumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. A nurse or doctor will give you this medicine in a clinic or hospital. Each infusion usually takes about 60 minutes. You will be watched closely during and after your infusion for any reactions. Do not try to give this medicine to yourself at home.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and the type of cancer being treated. It is usually given once every 2 weeks, but your schedule may be different depending on your treatment plan. Always follow your doctor's instructions exactly. Your dose may be slowed down or stopped if you have a reaction during the infusion.
missed_dose: If you miss or need to reschedule your infusion appointment, contact your doctor or clinic as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses. Your healthcare team will help you get back on the right schedule safely.
storage: Ramucirumab is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals in a clinic or hospital setting. You do not need to store this medicine at home. If you have any leftover medicine or supplies from a home infusion program, ask your pharmacist or nurse how to dispose of them safely.
what_to_avoid: Avoid activities that increase your risk of bleeding or injury, such as contact sports, since this medicine can affect your ability to stop bleeding. Avoid becoming pregnant while on this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use reliable birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine. Tell your doctor about all other medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take before starting treatment, as some may interact with ramucirumab.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or go to the emergency room right away if you experience: severe bleeding (such as coughing up blood, blood in your urine or stool, or unusual bruising), chest pain or pressure, sudden shortness of breath, signs of a stroke (sudden numbness, confusion, trouble speaking, or vision changes), severe headache, severe stomach pain, wound that will not heal, signs of an infusion reaction (flushing, chills, shaking, difficulty breathing, dizziness, or rash during or shortly after your infusion), very high blood pressure, swelling or pain in your legs, or fever with signs of infection. Also tell your doctor if you are planning any surgery or dental procedures, as you may need to temporarily stop this medicine.
when_it_works: Ramucirumab begins working to slow or stop cancer growth from the time you start treatment, but you may not notice any visible changes right away. Your doctor will use blood tests, scans, and check-ups to monitor how well the medicine is working. Some people see improvements within the first few months of treatment. Keep all your appointments even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine can cause serious harm to an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for 2 months after the last dose. Elderly patients (65 and older): Older adults may have a higher risk of certain side effects such as fatigue, swelling, and low sodium levels. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Let your doctor know if you have any kidney or liver problems, as your treatment may need to be adjusted. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children.
